I've written notes for all 15 verses, but there are gaps. I ran out of searches before I could open the Catholic and Orthodox sites, bibleodyssey.org, or the NET notes page itself. I also couldn't confirm Precept Austin's comments on vv. 8–15, because the fetched page was cut off after v. 2. I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, and nothing on "at noon" (v. 4) or the hissing (v. 15). Where tradition labels appear, they come from your site list, not from the pages.

## Zephaniah 2: verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- Guzik: the gathering is a solemn national act of mourning and repentance.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-2/
- Precept Austin: Judah has gone numb to its sin. Zephaniah calls it "nation," a word usually used for pagan peoples, to say Judah now looks no different from them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-2-commentary
- TGC: the Hebrew means roughly "the nation not longing" for God. The verb "gather" is normally used for collecting straw or sticks.  https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/zephaniah/
- NET note (quoted on Precept Austin): calling the people to gather like stubble is ironic. Straw is exactly what the Lord's fire burns up quickly (citing Adele Berlin). https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-2-commentary
- A different reading: the Moody Bible Commentary (quoted on Precept Austin) takes "gather" literally. It sees the Lord bringing Judah back to the land before a seven-year tribulation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-2-commentary

**v. 2**
- Guzik: the judgments of chapter 1 are a warning and an invitation.  He adds that the devil's strongest lie is often that there is no hurry. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-2/
- Matthew Henry: Zephaniah wanted not to frighten them out of their wits, but to frighten them out of their sins. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zep/Zep_002.cfm
- Precept Austin: "before" appears three times to press for action now.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-2-commentary
- TGC: "anger of the LORD" is also repeated, to stress how serious the need to repent is.  https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/zephaniah/

**v. 3**
- Guzik: even the righteous must take this warning to heart.  He links it to escaping the Great Tribulation (Luke 21:36). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-2/
- Henry: the "meek" are told to seek meekness.  On "it may be": God speaks doubtfully to test whether they will trust him and to keep them watchful. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zep/Zep_002.cfm
- Spurgeon (sermon notes on Precept Austin): this call to refuge is addressed to the meek, but it is our joy to proclaim a hiding-place for the guilty. People may seek the Lord on the faintest encouragement. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-2-commentary
- Gill: "seek the Lord" may mean seeking Christ for righteousness and life. He says the Vulgate's "seek the just, seek the meek One" refers to Christ himself. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/zephaniah/2-3.html and https://studylight.org/bible/msg/zephaniah/2-3.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/2-3.htm
- TGC: the Hebrew presents the remnant less as people who kept God's commands and more as those humbly taking his coming judgment seriously.  https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/zephaniah/
- Disagreement over who and when:
  - Chuck Smith suggests these may be people .
  - Coffman says the verse cannot mean only Israel's remnant. It reaches to the "second Israel" in Messiah's kingdom.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zephaniah/2-3.html
- Catholic and patristic voices (quoted by Barnes):
  - Dionysius says the "may be" does not express doubt. It shows how hard salvation is and how strict God's judgment is.
  - Jerome links the verse to Christ's "learn of me, for I am meek" (Matt 11:29).
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/2-3.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: judgment falls on unrepentant Judah, and also on the pagan nations around it.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-2/
- Precept Austin: "For" gives evidence that God's judgment is already moving toward fulfilment, which is why repentance is urgent. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-2-commentary

**v. 5**
- Guzik, quoting Baker: the name Cherethites points to the Philistines' early links with Crete. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-2/
- Precept Austin: when "the word of the LORD" is against someone, God himself has passed a legal verdict.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-2-commentary
- Henry:  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zep/Zep_002.cfm

**v. 6**
- Henry (on "no inhabitant"): God made the earth to be lived in. If people do not serve God, it is just for the earth to stop serving them as a home. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zep/Zep_002.cfm

**v. 7**
- Precept Austin:
  - Near meaning: the Jews who returned from exile in Babylon.
  - "Restore their fortunes" suggests both that return and a future remnant living in this area.
  - Walter Kaiser places this in the territory .
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-2-commentary
- Henry: the returned exiles will lie down safely in Ashkelon's houses in the evening, when they are tired. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zep/Zep_002.cfm

**v. 8**
- Henry: God takes personally the insults aimed at his people, because despising them dishonours him. He compares Ezek 25:3, 8. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zep/Zep_002.cfm

**v. 9**
- Guzik, quoting Walker: the Sodom and Gomorrah comparison fits Moab and Ammon's origins in Lot's daughters (Gen 19). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-2/
- Henry: a land once full of springs will grow only nettles and have brine pits instead. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zep/Zep_002.cfm
- Precept Austin: "perpetual desolation" means a ruin lasting for generations. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zephaniah-2-commentary

**v. 10**
- Henry:  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zep/Zep_002.cfm
- Bridgeway: in their pride they mocked God's people, and so mocked God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zephaniah/2-12.html

**v. 11** (the clearest split among the commentators)
- What "starve the gods" means:
  - Clarke: idol-worshippers thought their gods fed on the smoke of sacrifices. Here God cuts off the sacrifices. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zephaniah/2-11.html
  - Keil and Delitzsch: God makes the gods vanish by destroying the nations that relied on them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/2-11.htm
- Most read the worship of "every shore" as the spread of the gospel:
  - Henry says the "isles" include Britain, and that people will worship anywhere, without going to Jerusalem. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Zep/Zep_002.cfm
  - Poole:  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/2-11.htm
  - Barnes cites Pliny's report that pagan temples were nearly deserted within 80 years of Christ's death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/2-11.htm
- Disagreements:
  - Calvin's editor:  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zephaniah/2-11.html
  - David Levy (dispensational) places worship of God alone in the Millennium. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64260/
- Pulpit Commentary (application): to destroy idols is to withdraw people's highest love from everything short of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zephaniah-2.html

**v. 12**
- Guzik and the Pulpit Commentary: God looks in all four directions. Philistia is west, Moab and Ammon east, Cush south and Assyria north. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-2/ and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zephaniah-2.html
- The switch from "you" to "they":
  - Pulpit: 
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: it expresses estrangement from God.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/2-12.htm
- God's "sword" is Nebuchadnezzar, the human tool he used (JFB, Gill, Calvin, Constable). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/2-12.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zephaniah/2-12.html
- Disagreement over which Cushites are meant:
  - Poole and Gill: Arabian "Ethiopians" living near Moab. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/2-12.htm
  - Keil: distant African Ethiopia. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/2-12.htm
  - Gann: the Ethiopian dynasty that ruled Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zephaniah/2-12.html
  - Coffman rejects reading it as Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zephaniah/2-12.html
  - TGC notes that the Hebrew may refer to something other than a future event (the text was cut off). https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/zephaniah/
- Pulpit sees a fuller fulfilment when the Gospel reaches the far south, beginning with Candace's official (Acts 8:27). https://biblehub.com/zephaniah/2-12.htm

**v. 13**
- Pulpit: the ruin is God's own work ("he will stretch out his hand"), and it . https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zephaniah-2.html

**v. 14**
- The birds: older English versions have "cormorant and bittern," but the creatures are uncertain.
  - Calvin:  https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol29/htm/iv.iii.xii.htm
  - Pulpit: most recent critics read the second creature as a "hedgehog," as do the Septuagint and Vulgate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/2-14.htm
- Modern scholarship (Cambridge Bible): "cedar work" is a word found nowhere else, and . The Septuagint reads "ravens" for "desolation," which differs by one letter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/2-14.htm
- Pulpit: Assyrian monuments show cedar used in palaces. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zephaniah/2-14.htm
- Henry: a lesson about pride in grand buildings. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zephaniah/2-14.html

**v. 15**
- Guzik: Nineveh's boast shows that God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6). Zephaniah never says why the nations deserved judgment, perhaps because his readers already knew Amos, Isaiah and Nahum. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zephaniah-2/
- Pulpit: the prophet was moved by the instability of mere earthly greatness and might. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zephaniah-2.html

## Where the traditions differ

The main split I found is over when the "Day of the LORD" happens:
- **Dispensational/futurist readings:** Precept Austin, the Moody Bible Commentary, Chuck Smith, David Levy, and Guzik on enduringword.com (listed as Pentecostal/charismatic). They tie vv. 1–3, 7 and 11 to the Tribulation and the Millennium.
- **Already-and-not-yet:** TGC (listed as Reformed) says Christ's death brought the future day of the Lord into the middle of history, while its final completion is still to come. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/zephaniah/
- **Fulfilled in history and the gospel:** most older commentators. Calvin's editor dissents on v. 11.
